The Creator of the Egyptians was, then, represented in the form of a man, of an azure colour, who held a circle in one hand and in the other a royal rod, and on top of his head had a feather, which showed that the Creator of things, who is King, as the sceptre shows, can hardly be found, because it lies in his hand to give life to the universe, which he does while, understanding in himself, he revolves, and this the circle signifies that he holds in his hand.

From his mouth he sends out an egg, from which is born that god whom they call Vulcan. The egg signifies the World, and Vulcan that natural heat which in it gives life to things. Although in Egypt they showed the world with another idol as well, which was of a man with feet twisted together and tied; he had about him a garment that covered him down to the feet, all varied and of different colours; and he bore on his head a great golden ball. These things signified that the World is round and never changes place, and that the nature of the stars is changeable.

Image of the Creator God of the Egyptians and of Jupiter, god of the gods of the ancient heathens, which denote the nature of God and his providence, goodness, communication and governance of all things.
Universe depicted
Serpents held to be of divine nature

All this is said by Porphyry, as Eusebius reports, who writes also that the Universe was painted by the Egyptians in this way. They drew two circles one above the other, and crossed them with a serpent that had the head of a hawk. The circles showed the size and shape of the World, and the serpent the good Daemon, preserver of everything, who comprehends the universe by his power, that is, that spirit which gives it life and nourishes it; for the Phoenicians and the Egyptians held that serpents are of divine nature, seeing that these, not with the help of external limbs, as other animals do, but moved only by their spirit and liveliness, go very swiftly and with marvellous quickness twist and retwist the body in various ways; besides which they live a very long time, because they lay aside old age together with the skin which they change, and so, made young again, they seem unable ever to die of themselves, unless perhaps they are killed. And they added the head of the hawk as well, for its quickness and great agility.
Martianus Capella
Image of Jupiter

Martianus Capella, when in the wedding of Mercury and Philologia he imagines that Jupiter calls all the other gods to a council, describes him thus. On his head he has a royal crown, all resplendent and flaming; a shining veil, once woven by the hand of Pallas, covers the nape of his neck; he is dressed all in white, except that above he has a mantle, which seems of glass, painted with sparkling stars; in his right hand he holds two round balls, one of gold, the other of gold and silver; and in the left a lyre with nine strings; his shoes are of green emerald, and he sits upon a cloth made and woven of peacock feathers, and with his feet he treads on a trident.

Image of Jupiter, god of the gods of the ancients, signifying the power and providence of God, and that he is the maker and preserver of all things, and that from him comes the harmony of the celestial spheres.

Statues of Jupiter were also made in such a way that they not only signified who he was and what he could do, but also gave to understand what men ought to do among themselves, and chiefly Kings and Princes toward their subjects: for these (as I remember having said at another time) are on earth as it were the image of God, and therefore ought, as far as they are able, to represent likewise the providence, justice and goodness of God.
Plutarch
Jupiter without ears
Jupiter with four ears

Plutarch writes, then, that in Crete there was once an idol of Jupiter which had no ears, to show that he who is over others and has to govern them ought not to listen to what is said to him, neither this more than that, nor that more than this, but to stand so firm and steady that he never departs from the straight path because of other people's words. And on the contrary the Lacedaemonians depicted him with four ears, as though Jupiter heard everything and understood everything, or else because he must have two ears to judge, in order to hear one party, and two for the other: which likewise refers to the prudence of the King and the Prince, who has to hear and understand everyone, and all that his peoples do.
Jupiter with three eyes

And perhaps the same thing was meant to be shown by the one who once depicted Jupiter with three eyes, as though he saw everything and nothing were hidden from him: as nothing ought to be hidden either from him who has the care and government of cities. Hence it came about that the ancients said that justice sees everything, as appears in her image.
Pausanias
Aeschylus

But Pausanias gives another reason for it, writing that among the Argives, in the temple of Minerva, there was an idol of Jupiter which had two eyes, as one sees men have, and another in the middle of its forehead; and he says one may think that this signified that Jupiter has three kingdoms to watch over. One is that of Heaven, because everyone commonly reputed him King of Heaven; another is that of Hell, that is of the Earth, because the Earth, in respect of Heaven, is Hell, and Homer for this reason calls him infernal Jupiter; the third is that of the sea, because Aeschylus calls him King of the Sea; and Martianus Capella (as I have said above) puts the trident under his feet; and Orpheus, in a certain hymn, prays Justice to take care of all the living, who are nourished by mother Earth and by marine Jupiter.

The three eyes in Jupiter show, then, according to Pausanias, that those three kingdoms of the universe are subject to him, which the fables say he divided with his other two brothers, the kingdom of the Sea falling to Neptune and that of Hell to Pluto. That in the statues of the gods the ancients showed by the eye what the office of the ruler was is seen, Plutarch again says, from what the Egyptians did, who among their sacred paintings, when they wished to represent the King, drew a sceptre with an eye at the top, as I have already said that they painted the Sun too, and they depicted Jupiter likewise with the same figure, wishing by this to be understood that, as the King can do much, because the sceptre is a sign of superiority and of the power one has over others, so he must be vigilant in the government of his peoples, always showing himself just in all his affairs.
Suda
Aristotle

We read also that beside the statue of Jupiter the ancients used to place that of Justice, as though the King never did, or never ought to do, anything that was not accompanied by Justice. Hence the ancients also used, as Suda reports, to put a stork at the top of sceptres and a hippopotamus at the butt, wishing in this way to show that the King must be pious and just, and must crush those who with violence and unjustly do harm to others. For we read, and Aristotle confirms it, that the stork feeds its father and mother after they have grown old, in the same way that it was once fed and reared by them, a most pious and most just act; and the hippopotamus is so impious and unjust, as Plutarch writes, that it does violence to its father and kills him, and afterwards consorts with its mother.
Plutarch

Besides this we read in the same Plutarch that in Thebes there were some statues without hands, which represented the judges and the administrators of justice, because these must be without hands, that is, they must in no way accept reward or gifts, on account of which they would then have to wrong someone, ruling in favour of one who has no right. And among these there was another without eyes, which represented the ruler who is over the judges, because he must be free from every passion, both hatred and love, considering only in himself what is just, without having regard more to this man than to that in having justice administered, as Kings and Princes are bound to do, as well as officials and magistrates, not only by the law of nature but by their own oath as well.

And by doing otherwise, both the one and the other must expect to be punished by Jupiter, the chastiser of perjury, as the ancients showed in his statues too: for we read that among the Eleans, a people of Greece, there was one which was very frightening and greatly feared by treacherous men and perjurers. It held the thunderbolt in both hands, as though it stood ready to punish the perjurer.
Water of Jupiter of perjury

Aristotle also tells of a certain water, writing of the marvellous things of the world, that it was in Cappadocia near Tyana, the chief city of that country, and that at its spring it was very cold but there seemed to boil. If someone was brought to it about whom there was doubt whether he had sworn falsely, then, if he had spoken the truth, it showed itself calm and went on with a slow and pleasant course; but if the man had sworn a lie, it showed itself so angry against him that, swelling up, it flung itself at his feet, his hands and even his face, as though it wished to punish him for his perjury, and it never left him until he had openly confessed his sin and, weeping, begged pardon for it, or (if he stayed obstinate) became dropsical there and vomited from his mouth a great quantity of blood, all corrupt and spoiled; and so the Greeks called this the water of Jupiter of perjury.
Image of Fidelity signified by the god Dius Fidius, worshipped in antiquity. Truth is represented here as Mother, Honour as Father, Love as the bond.

And among the Corinthians, Pausanias writes, there was in the temple of Neptune a secret chamber with an entrance that ran underground, where they said Portunus dwelt, and whoever had sworn falsely there, whoever he might be, could not escape being punished at once. And the Eleans likewise went to swear at the altar of Sosipolis, their god, with great reverence.
Ceremony of swearing

Pausanias does not relate the ceremony they used there; but he does tell, in another place, the one they performed at the much-celebrated Olympic games, where people gathered from every side, some to run on foot, some to race horses, some to wrestle, and some for other things; for whoever won there was highly esteemed, so that great care had to be taken that no deceit should be practised there. And for this reason not only those who went to take part in any of those games, but their fathers too, their brothers and the trainers who had exercised them, all of whom went to accompany them, swore with certain solemn words over the testicles of a pig, which for this purpose were solemnly cut off there at that moment, that they would commit no fraud.

And the competitors swore besides that they had trained for ten continuous months in that kind of contest for which they had come. And those who were to judge the victory swore likewise that they would take no gift [?] from the competitors or from their people, that they would not favour one more than another in any way, and that they would not reveal why they approved or rejected this one more than that one.
qm: “they would take no gift [?]” — the print has “doro”, which can be read as “dono” (gift) or “d’oro” (of gold, any gold); translated as “gift”.

blocks.text: And because this was almost in the form of a sacrifice, and in sacrifices it was the custom to eat the flesh of the sacrificed animals, Pausanias added that he does not know what was done with this pig, on whose testicles the solemn oath had been made, but that he knows well that the ancient religion forbade eating the flesh of the victim over which an oath had been solemnly sworn, as is seen in Homer, when he says that the priest threw into the sea the pig on whose testicles Agamemnon swore that he had not touched Briseis. And almost similar was the ceremony the Romans used in making truces, for they swore and made certain imprecations over a pig which they had there, in the presence of the priests appointed for the purpose.
Jupiter Horcius
Dius Fidius

But leaving the ceremonies, let us return to the god who guards the oath, called by the Greeks Jupiter Horcius and represented in a statue that held the thunderbolt in both hands. He was depicted by the Romans in another way and also named otherwise, although the numen was the same, as some have said of Jupiter Horcius and of the Roman god Dius Fidius, because just as the former watched over the oath, that it should be true and just, so the latter presided over the keeping of faith, and for this reason he was worshipped, and he is found among the antiquities of Rome made in this way.

Image of Jupiter hurling thunderbolts against perjurers, called Jupiter Horcius, guardian of the oath and severe chastiser and destroyer of those who swear falsely and of those who were ready to swear.

Image of the god Dius Fidius, guardian of faith and fidelity; of Jupiter called Vejovis, that is harmful and punishing, in the dress of Bacchus, to whom his numen is attributed; and of the Goat Amalthea, who gave milk to Jupiter, from one of whose horns the horn of plenty, or cornucopia, was made.
blocks.pt: Вейовис и Юпитер в облачении Вакха

blocks.text: It is a piece of marble carved in the manner of a window, on which are sculpted three figures from the middle upward, of which the one on the right side is a man in peaceful dress, and beside him are letters saying HONOR; the other, on the left side, is a woman in the same dress, with a laurel wreath on her head, and with letters saying VERITAS. These two figures give each other the right hand, and between them is the third, a boy with a beautiful and honest face, over whose head are carved those two words DIVS FIDIVS.
Vejovis
Gellius
Horn of plenty

And as for Jupiter punishing the perjurer, as I have said, it comes to my mind that he was not always worshipped in order that he should help (*giouasse*), but also sometimes in order that he should not harm; and then they called him Vejovis, as though he could only harm. They showed this too in his statue, for they depicted it, as we read in Gellius and as Alexander ab Alexandro reports, in the form of a boy with horns on his head and arrows in his hand, as if about to strike, and beside him was a goat.

For the fables said that his mother, to save him from the voracious throat of Saturn, had given him into the keeping of two nymphs in Crete, one named Amalthea and the other Melissa, or else Aega and Helice, and these nursed him with honey and the milk of a goat of theirs which they loved dearly. It happened one day that this goat unluckily broke a horn against a tree, to the very great displeasure of the nymphs, who were beyond measure grieved; and, being unable to do anything else, they filled it with various flowers and fruits and, having adorned it all with beautiful leaves, presented it to Jupiter, who held it very dear and wished that, in honour of his nurse, it should always be a sign of abundance; so we call it the horn of plenty, and sometimes also the horn of Amalthea, of which Pherecydes said, as Apollodorus reports, that its virtue is such that it gives abundantly all that a man can desire for food and drink.

We read also that this horn was not the goat's but an ox's, and that ox into which Achelous changed himself when he once fought with Hercules for Deianira, who had been promised by her father to both; for Hercules, as the fables say, broke it off and threw it away; but the Naiads, nymphs of the rivers, picked it up and, having filled it with various flowers and fruits and adorned it with green leaves, consecrated it to Copia, which is understood as the goddess of abundance, and for this reason it was called the Horn of Copia and of Plenty.
The cornucopia and its interpretation

This (leaving aside the histories that lie beneath this fable) some say shows the power of fortune, because many animals have all their strength in their horns and often wound with them; and fortune has abundance as her minister, because she is exceedingly rich, and it lies as it were in her hand to give and to take away riches and temporal goods.

Image of Jupiter surrounded by the three Graces and the three Horae, whose throne is upheld by images of Victory, with a crowned Victory in one hand and the sceptre with the eagle in the other, signifying the absolute dominion of God and that all things are subject to him.

The abundance of flowers and fruits therefore lies in the horn of plenty (whether it was a goat's or an ox's), because riches and the other worldly goods seem to be in the power of fortune, and to go and come as it pleases her. It might also be said that the horn of plenty came from the goat that gave milk to Jupiter, because all goods were believed to come from him, as I have already said. Hence he was given the same power that the Sun has, and for this reason they wished him to have arrows in his hand in the statue that I drew a little while ago.
Jupiter with the ornaments of Bacchus
Eagle of Jupiter

And some gave him likewise the numen of Bacchus, making an idol of him with the ornaments of Bacchus, as Pausanias relates that Polykleitos made one in Arcadia, which had buskins on its feet and with one hand held a drinking vessel and with the other a thyrsus, at the top of which was an eagle. And this one too had to be young, as Bacchus is depicted; as was also the Jupiter worshipped at Terracina, to whom they gave a surname that means without a razor, because he was beardless and had no need of such a knife. Few are the statues of Jupiter to which an eagle is not added in some way, as his own bird.
Eagle queen of birds

And for this reason the chariot of Jupiter is always drawn by eagles, either because, as Lactantius reports, he took a good omen of victory from the eagle that once appeared to him while he was going to a certain war (and some say it was against Saturn), from which he returned victorious; and so it was afterwards feigned that in the war against the Giants the eagle supplied Jupiter with arms, and for this reason they often paint it with him carrying the thunderbolt in its talons; or else because we read that of all birds the eagle alone is safe from the bolt of Heaven, and that it alone likewise fixes its eyes on the Sun; so that with reason it is called the queen of birds and given to Jupiter, likewise King of the gods.
Jupiter on the throne

We find Jupiter also (as Phidias made him for the Eleans, and Pausanias describes him) of gold and ivory, seated on a fine royal throne, with a crown on his head made of olive leaves. In his right hand he has a Victory, likewise crowned, and in the left a sceptre made of various metals, which has an eagle at the top; the mantle he wears is of gold, worked with various animals and with flowers of every sort, but for the most part lilies, and the shoes likewise are gilded.
Jupiter Custos
Lucian

On the throne, which is all gleaming with gold and precious stones, made of ivory and ebony, many animals are carved, besides the three Graces, who are on one side above the head of the idol, and three Horae on the other, and four images of Victory support it in place of feet. Jupiter is likewise seated on a high throne on an ancient medal of Nero, and has the thunderbolt in his right hand and a spear in his left, with letters saying Jupiter Custos. And Lucian, writing of the Syrian Goddess, says that in the temple of this goddess there was an idol of Jupiter placed seated on two bulls.
Image of Jupiter with the Thunderbolt and with the Spear, to show the stability of the government of divine Providence and at the same time its prompt punishment of the evil deeds of the wicked.
Jupiter Stator

But on the other hand, on some medals likewise ancient, of Antoninus Pius and of Gordian, Jupiter stands nude, on his feet, and has the spear in his right hand and the thunderbolt in his left, with letters saying Jupiter Stator. He was so called in a certain temple built for him by Romulus, because at his prayers he stopped the Roman soldiers and, making them turn about, made them stand firm, when once, fighting against the Sabines, they had taken to flight.
Jupiter Conservator

Not very unlike this is Jupiter Conservator, who is seen on the ancient medals of Diocletian, who likewise stands upright and has in his right hand two arrows, so that they can be taken also for two thunderbolts, and a spear in his left. And on another medal of the same Diocletian he is called Jupiter Conservator of the universe, and he holds the spear with the left hand and with the right offers a small image of Victory.
Thunderbolt of Summanus
Thunderbolt given to several gods
Minerva hurls the thunderbolt

No other emblem seems to be so proper to Jupiter as the thunderbolt, although the Romans gave it, as Pliny writes, to the god Summanus as well, who was the same as Pluto, but only the one that came by night, because the thunderbolt of the day was Jupiter's. The Etruscans, most ancient observers of these things, maintained that Vulcan and Minerva likewise hurl the thunderbolt, with which, we read, she once burned the fleet of the Greeks.
Virgil
Hence in Virgil Juno, indignant within herself at being unable to do the harm that she wished to Aeneas and the other Trojans when, after the ruin of Troy, they were going to Italy, says thus:

lines: Pallas was able to take vengeance
on the Greeks and burn their ships,
hurling upon them with her own hand
from the lofty clouds the thunderbolt of Jupiter:
And I, &c.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: Thunderbolts of three colours
Acron

And they said that the thunderbolts hurled by the other gods (for so we shall interpret, for now, what they called Manubiae) were white or black; but red was the one that came from the hand of Jupiter, as Acron reports, where Horace says that the supreme father with his burning right hand has touched the sacred towers.
Thunderbolt of three kinds
Marvels of the thunderbolt
Marcia

From this come the three kinds of thunderbolt set down by Aristotle, of which one is so clear and penetrating that it works the miracles that are read of as too great, for instance that, passing through, it drinks all the wine of a cask without leaving any sign of having touched the cask; that it melts silver and any other metal it finds in chests without at all harming the chests; that in Marcia, a Roman woman, it destroyed the child she still bore in her womb and did her no harm; that it kills people, and it is not seen to have touched the clothes they have on, and other similar things: and this kind of thunderbolt comes from Minerva, who was born from the head of Jupiter, and is therefore the most purified and subtlest part of fire, and it will be the white one. The other burns whatever it finds, and let this be the red, sent by the hand of Jupiter. The third, which has more of the moist and the coarse, does not burn but only stains, and for that reason they called it black and gave it to Vulcan, minister of this our fire, all smoky.
Image of Jupiter hurling thunderbolts and bringing rains and storm clouds, and image of Zeus Labrandeus of the Lydians, signifying that God is prepared to punish evildoers, and divine providence.

For these reasons the poets called the thunderbolt three-forked, as one that strikes in three ways, and it is likewise painted with three points, and there were three Cyclopes who forged it, as is told in the image of Vulcan; to whom, however, I do not find that the thunderbolt was ever given, either in statue or in painting, and still less to Minerva; although what I have written of it is read, to show its nature and its various effects; but to Jupiter alone they have given it, sometimes in his hand and sometimes at his feet; now the eagle brings it to him close by with its beak, now with its claws, and in various other ways it has been carved and painted.
Seneca

Seneca says that giving Jupiter the thunderbolt, with which he often frightens the World, was a fiction of the ancients to curb the rashness of arrogant ignorant men, who would have given themselves licentiously to every sort of wickedness if they had feared no one who exceeded all human strength. To frighten, therefore, those who could do good only out of fear, it was said that Jupiter, supreme judge of human actions, stood over them with his right hand armed with the thunderbolt.

Nor did he always hurl it of his own will alone: but, as I have said already, often with the counsel of the other gods; and it was then most grave, and a bringer of many ills, just as it was light, and showed that the anger of Jupiter could easily be appeased, when the heavenly counsel did not intervene.
Moral lesson

From this Seneca draws a very fine moral lesson, saying that, just as Jupiter, supreme King of the gods, benefits mortals and sends them good without asking the counsel of the other gods, so among us Kings and other lords ought, before doing harm to others, whether as punishment or for any other reason whatever, to think it over carefully and take good counsel, remembering that Jupiter does not trust his own judgment alone when he has to send some grave evil to the world, and that it was said that of the thunderbolts sent by Jupiter some were heavy and destructive and some light and of little harm for no other reason than to give to understand to him whose business it is to punish human errors that he should not strike all in the same way, nor show himself equally terrible to everyone.
Aegis carried by Jupiter
Virgil

We read also that Jupiter carried on his left arm the skin of the goat that nursed him when he was still a baby, called the aegis, and that by shaking it he made the rains, just as with his right he hurled the thunderbolt, as Servius notes on Virgil, where he says that the Arcadians believed they had seen, from the very beginning, Jupiter himself around the Tarpeian Rock:

lines: When he often shakes the black aegis,
and with his right hand stirs the dark storm clouds.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: Diphthera, book of Jupiter

And that on the same skin, also called Diphthera, he wrote everything that was done throughout the universe, so as not to forget anything, when he wished to review the account of human actions. Hence the ancients used to say as a proverb that Jupiter had indeed looked once into the Diphthera, when they saw some wicked man, after having been happy for a time, punished at last and chastised for his wicked deeds.
Plutarch

Moreover, Jupiter was depicted without a thunderbolt too, as we read that there was an idol of him in Caria, a region of Asia Minor, which had neither thunderbolt nor sceptre nor anything else of what has been described so far, but only an axe, and the reason for it is given. Plutarch relates that Hercules, having killed Hippolyta, Queen of the Amazons, took the axe which she carried among her other arms, and gave it to his Omphale, who was a Lydian, and therefore the Kings of Lydia afterwards used to carry it, and guarded it as a sacred thing.
Candaules
Zeus Labrandeus

It passed through the hands of many Kings to Candaules, who then did not deign to carry it but had it carried by one who was always with him, who together with Candaules was killed by Gyges, the winner of the war that he had previously begun against him, and among the other spoils which he brought back to Caria was the axe too, which he then put in the hand of an idol of Jupiter made there for this purpose, which was called Labrandeus, because those of Lydia call the axe *labra*.
Inventors of the equipment of war

But Lactantius holds that he was so called from one named Labrandeus who brought help to Jupiter and aided him in a very great war. To this idol, Aelian says, a knife was also hung, called Carian, and it was greatly revered, because they say that the Carians were the first to make those things which serve for war: to fight for reward, to fit shields so that they could be carried on the arm, and to put crests on helmets.
Jupiter giving birth

And because painters often show the fables, painting them as well as the poets have invented them in writing, a pupil of Apelles, having once heard, or perhaps read, that Jupiter gave birth to Bacchus, painted him, as Pliny writes, with certain ornaments which the women of Lydia wore on their heads, in the midst of some women who were helping him to give birth, and he, like a woman who feels great pain in labour, seemed to be lamenting, and there were many goddesses there, who were making the greatest hubbub in the world.
Pausanias

I do not tell of Bacchus, how Jupiter carried him for a time attached to his side, until the hour of mature birth came, because these fables from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* are by now so common that everyone knows them. The ancient sculptors likewise have often taken from the poets the example for the statues they have made. Hence Pausanias writes that certain Leontines, a people of Greece, at their own private expense made a Jupiter seven cubits high, which had an eagle in its left hand, and carried a dart with its right, because they had already seen him so described by some poets.
Strabo
Homer

Strabo tells of the temple of Olympian Jupiter, which on account of the oracle that was there was once celebrated for a time in such a way that from every part of Greece people flocked there to bring many rich gifts, as Cypselus, tyrant of Corinth, did, who offered there an idol of Jupiter all of solid gold; and he says that in it there was a statue of Jupiter too, made of ivory by Phidias the Athenian, so great that although the temple was very large, it was nevertheless small for the greatness of the statue. For this reason the artist seemed to have ill observed the proportion of the place, because he made it so that, seated, it touched the high roof with its head, so that if it had stood up it would have had to be broken through, since it was much taller than the temple. But it was not for this less praised than its beauty deserved, for Quintilian writes that this seemed to add something, I know not what, to religion and to the reverence that was borne to Jupiter, so well did it represent the divine majesty, of which Phidias (as he said to Pandaenus his nephew, who asked him) took the example from Homer, where he says thus:

lines: With a grave and reverend nod
the son of Saturn showed his will.
Moving his head, which, sprinkled with ambrosia,
made the universe move together.
blocks.author: Homer

blocks.text: The painters too have sometimes invented something of their own, as Apelles did when he was accused of the conspiracy, as can be seen in the image of Calumny. And Pliny writes that Nealces, a painter of great genius, had painted a naval war between the Egyptians and the Persians, and, not being able by the painting of the places alone to show that it had been fought on the Nile, as he wished it to be understood, he thought of showing this in the following way. He painted an ass drinking on the bank, and a crocodile lying in wait to do it harm, because the crocodile is an animal proper to Egypt, and in Persia there is a great abundance of asses.
Sicyonians

For which reasons I wish to say that it was perhaps an invention of the painters too, or of the sculptors, to make the images of the gods without any form of man or of other animal, as it is read of Venus that she had one in Paphos; the Sun likewise was so represented among the Phoenicians; and the Sicyonians, a people of the Morea, had a Jupiter made in the shape of a pyramid, as Pausanias writes.

Image of the oracle of Jupiter Ammon of the Troglodytes, signifying the obscurity and baseness of worldly things, and that one must look, and raise oneself with the keenness of the intellect, to the height of the divine.

This, I believe, is meant to signify the same thing that the statue of the same Jupiter (of which I have already spoken) also signifies, nude from the middle upward and clothed in the rest. For the base of these images represents to us the gloom of the darkness through which we walk in this world, so that, keeping our mind applied to human things, we cannot have any knowledge of the divine, into which we must look with the keenness of the mind, shown by the sharp top of the pyramid. And our mind can do this when it cuts away all the effects of the body and grows subtle so as to penetrate the Heavens; or when it lays down the corporeal mass and, all unburdened and light, flies back to enjoy the blessed vision of eternal things.
Quintus Curtius
Jupiter Ammon
Fountain of the Sun
Image in the form of a navel

And therefore, whether this or something else was the cause, Quintus Curtius writes that among the Troglodytes in Egypt, where there was a grove consecrated to the god Ammon, who was Jupiter, in the middle of which rose a spring called the water of the Sun (which, as Pomponius Mela also reports, at the beginning of the day was lukewarm, at midday cold; towards evening it grew a little warm, and at midnight was so hot that it boiled, and towards day it gradually grew lukewarm), a certain thing was worshipped which was not such as the idols of the gods are usually made, but in the form of a navel composed of emeralds and other gems, wide below and round, tapering towards the top. When they wished to learn something from it, the priests carried it, wrapped up, on a little gilded boat, to which many silver cups were attached all around, and women and girls went within it, singing certain unmetrical verses, by which they thought to make Jupiter give them afterwards certain answers about what they wished to know.
Jupiter in the form of a Ram

Under the image of a ram this Jupiter Ammon was also worshipped, and some say the cause of it was this: when Bacchus was once walking through the deserts of Libya, he was on the point of perishing of thirst with all his army, if, after pious prayers to the Father, a ram had not come, which, always going before him, led him where he found enough to water the whole army; and believing that Jupiter had come in that animal to show him the desired waters, he set up an altar there and made his idol in the form of a ram.
Herodotus

Ovid, following the fables, holds that this was because, when the gods of Heaven fled from the fury of the Giants into Egypt, Jupiter, for his greater safety, changed himself there into a ram. And Herodotus, giving the reason why the Thebans in Egypt were forbidden to sacrifice sheep, writes that Jupiter, not wishing to be seen by Hercules, who greatly desired it and begged him for it every day, and being no longer able to resist such affectionate entreaties, showed himself to him dressed in a ram's skin; and that from this the Egyptians then took the idol of Jupiter in the form of a ram.

Image of Jupiter Ammon of the Arcadians and of the Egyptians, and of the oak and the ram sacred to him, signifying that God is the author of life and the sustainer of the living, and the doubtful answers of the said oracle of Ammon.
Ram revered

This animal is greatly revered among them, and they never kill it for sacrifice, except on the day of the festival of Jupiter, on which every year they cut off the head of a ram and flay it, clothing the idol of Jupiter in that skin, to which they then bring that of Hercules, so that he may see it; and finally all who are there go to beat the flayed ram and, having put it in a sacred urn, bury it with the greatest reverence. This Jupiter Ammon was not only in Egypt, but in Greece too, and among the Arcadians (as Pausanias recounts) he was made in a square form in the manner of the Herms, statues of Mercury, and had on his head the horns of a ram, and some also gave him the whole head of a ram, and this because his answers were as doubtful as is the head of a ram wrapped in that skin of its own.
Alexander ab Alexandro

Besides this we find, as Alexander ab Alexandro reports, that the Celts, a people of Gaul, set up as the image and statue of Jupiter a very tall oak, and worshipped it as Jupiter, perhaps because they knew that among trees the oak was consecrated to Jupiter, as the one from whose fruit men lived in the earliest times, and that it was for him to feed and nourish those whom he was believed to have produced into the world and over whom he had the universal government. For this reason the ancients crowned with oak almost all the statues of Jupiter, as though the oak were a sign of life, which was believed to be given by him to mortals. Hence the Romans used to give a crown of oak to one who in war had defended a Roman citizen from death, wishing to give him, who had been the cause of another's living, the badge of life.
Pausanias

But of olive too they sometimes made wreaths for Jupiter, because it is always green and very useful to mortals, and its leaves seem almost the colour of Heaven, although it is held rather to be the tree of Pallas, or Minerva, who is the same, as can be seen in her image. And Pausanias writes that in a certain part of Greece there was an idol of Jupiter which held a bird in one hand and in the other the thunderbolt, and had on its head a fine wreath of various spring flowers.
Martianus Capella
Servius

Jupiter also often had the crown of a King, according to the way Martianus Capella describes him above. For, as Pallas depicted him when contending with Arachne in Ovid, the image of Jupiter is regal, since he was believed to be King of the gods, of men and of the universe. And Servius, on the tenth Eclogue of Virgil, says that the proper insignia of Jupiter, which those who celebrated a triumph used to wear, were the sceptre and the toga palmata, which was a large, ample garment of purple, in which some have said that the palm was woven on the inside, and others that it was painted with large golden bosses. The sceptre was of ivory with an eagle on top, and this is taken from Juvenal in Satire X and from Prudentius in the Hymn of St Romanus the Martyr. The portrait is seen on the ancient medals of the Emperor Probus and on some consular ones, as they call them.
Pliny

That the face was painted red on him was because, as Pliny also writes, the Romans on every festival used to tint the face of Jupiter with red lead, and it was one of the principal things the censors did, to give Jupiter out to be coloured with red lead. And those who celebrated a triumph likewise made themselves all red with red lead; from this women took the custom, which has since come down to our times, of making themselves coloured and red, thinking they become more beautiful, whereas many often make themselves frightening to look at. And in Ethiopia likewise the great men used to paint not only the face but the whole body with red lead, and gave the same colour to all the idols of their gods.
Victims of Jupiter
Mad ceremony
Axe summoned to judgment

There were then victims of Jupiter, sacrificed to him by the Romans for various reasons, at various times, and under various surnames: the goat, the two-year-old ewe lamb, and a white bull with gilded horns; although they also sometimes sacrificed without a victim, with spelt, salt and incense. Among the Athenians an ox was sacrificed to him, with a very ridiculous ceremony, and it was as Pausanias recounts. They put a little spelt and wheat mixed together on the altar of Jupiter, and the ox destined for the sacrifice, approaching it, went to eat it; then one of the priests, called by the Greeks, from the office he held, Bouphonos, which in our language means striker of the ox, having dealt that beast a blow on the head with an axe, at once ran away, leaving the axe there, which was then summoned to judgment by those who were round about, as though they had not seen anyone else wound the ox but the axe.
Suda

This custom, as Suda writes, came from what once happened at a certain festival of Jupiter, at which an ox ate the flat cakes that were ready for the sacrifice; at which one who was present there, annoyed, thinking that beast had been too presumptuous, seized an axe and killed it, and ran away. The axe that remained was summoned to judgment, and the judges, having heard the arguments of the parties, acquitted it; and it was afterwards observed to do the same every year. And it is no great wonder that an axe was summoned to judgment among the Athenians, because among the first laws that were given them by Draco was that even inanimate things, as Pausanias and Suda report, when the person who had done the harm was not found, should be condemned in court, banished, and thrown outside the city according to their deserts.

Hence in the same authors one and the same tale is read, although the names differ, because Pausanias writes of Theagenes, and Suda of Nicon. This man (whatever name he had) was so valiant that from the victories won in various places he had brought back more than four hundred crowns, and a fine statue was therefore erected to him, to which, after he was dead, one who had always been envious of his honours used to go at night and beat it well with a whip; and he was as pleased with it as if he had offended Theagenes or Nicon still alive.

It happened that the statue fell suddenly upon the one who was beating it, and killed him, whereupon his sons summoned it to judgment, and said so much against it that they had it condemned as guilty of their father's death, and it was therefore thrown into the sea. For this reason, soon afterwards, a great sterility came, which ruined the whole country; which was remedied by the advice of the oracle by restoring to its place the statue thrown into the sea and afterwards found by some fishermen; and divine honours were then also given to it, and it was worshipped as a saving numen.
Various transformations of Jupiter

The many fables too that are read of Jupiter give occasion to represent him in many ways; for they relate that he often changed himself into various forms to enjoy his loves: as when he changed into a white bull to carry off Europa, into an eagle to ravish Ganymede, and also to have Asteria; into a golden rain to reach Danaë; into a swan to be with Leda; into fire to deceive Aegina; into Amphitryon to lie with Alcmene; into Diana to enjoy Callisto, and into many other shapes, both bestial and human; of which I shall say nothing more, because I do not find that the ancients ever took an example from these to make any image of Jupiter.
Sister of Jupiter

Those who said that the ancients, under the names of various gods, worshipped the elements took Juno to be the air, and the fables therefore afterwards made her the sister of Jupiter, by whom they understood the element of fire. And as he is king, so they called her queen of Heaven, because fire and air are the two upper elements, which have far greater force in created things than the other two.
Wife of Jupiter
Virgil

And at times they also said that she was the earth, and therefore the wife of Jupiter; for they hold that from the higher bodies there falls to earth a certain seminal virtue, which gives it the power to produce everything that it produces, just as a husband, spreading his seed in the womb of his wife, makes her conceive what she afterwards bears in her time. For which reason Virgil said:

lines: Great Jupiter descended with fertile rains
into the bosom of his joyful wife.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: Eyebrows guarded by Juno

And some, wishing to place this goddess still higher, made her one and the same with the Moon, and gave her some of the Moon's epithets: thus they called her Lucina, as if it were she who, by helping women in childbirth, gave light (*luce*) to the children being born. From this it came about that the ancients, when they divided the human body and gave each god his own part to take care of, placed the eyebrows under the guardianship of Juno, because these are above the eyes, by which we enjoy the light that is given to us by her, and they seem to defend them from whatever might fall and come to trouble them.

Though we also read that the arms were likewise consecrated to her. Hence in Homer, who gives each god one limb more beautiful than the others, Juno has beautiful, white arms. And from this it came about that some of the ancients represented her with a clean and pure body, having regard, perhaps, to the body of the Moon.
Lucian
Syrian Goddess

Lucian writes that although the Syrian Goddess, so greatly revered at Hierapolis, a city of Assyria, was Juno, nevertheless her statue, which stood there in her temple, showed her to be not one only but many, since one saw in it something of Pallas, something of Venus, of Diana, of Nemesis, of the Parcae and of other goddesses; for she sat upon two lions, and held a sceptre in one hand and a spindle in the other, and on her head had certain rays and certain other things that are proper to different images. Hence Lucian in effect shows that the Syrian Goddess, that is, Juno, was a numen worshipped in different ways under different names.

Image of Juno Lucina, and of the Syrian Goddess of Hierapolis in Assyria, who is one and the same as Juno; and of the birds sacred to her, signifying that Juno is queen of Heaven, ruler of the air, lady of kingdoms and of riches. She was understood also as virtue.
And so it is no wonder that she was believed to be Lucina as well, and that women called on her for help in childbirth, as Glycerium does in Terence when she cries out:

lines: Juno Lucina, help me, and guard me, I pray you, from death.
blocks.author: Terence

blocks.text: And when they wished to make statues of her, or to paint her, the ancients depicted her, as can be seen on the ancient medals of Faustina, in the form of a woman of already mature age, dressed in the manner of a matron, who holds a cup in her right hand and a spear in her left.

And there are few images of the gods to which the ancients did not give spears, as can be seen in those already described, and will be seen again in those that remain to be described; and so it does not seem to me that I should put off giving the reason any longer. Though perhaps it would have been better elsewhere, still it will not be amiss to give it here too, where someone could easily be surprised that a spear is given to Juno, a peaceful and quiet goddess.
Homer

But she was not always such; on the contrary, at times she has shown herself very terrible and fierce, as when with all her strength she wished to help the Greeks against the Trojans and dared to go into battle together with Minerva, as Homer relates, who paints her chariot in this way because in those times commanders and the most distinguished persons fought in chariots. The beam that supported it crosswise was of iron; the wheels were of copper and had eight similar spokes, but the rims that go around them were of gold, covered on the outside with copper, and the hub from which these spokes came out was encircled with silver. Above, where the goddess stood, was a seat made with straps of gold and silver; the pole was of silver, the yoke of gold, and likewise of gold were the ornaments of the horses, because although at other times Juno had herself drawn by birds, then she needed horses.
And Virgil likewise gives her a chariot and arms, when he says that she loved Carthage so well that she kept her chariot and her arms there.

So it should not seem wrong to anyone that the ancients gave a spear to Juno also, nor that I, speaking of her, say why spears were given to the statues of the gods, according to the reason Justin gives for it, who says that in the earliest times kings carried a spear in place of the diadem and the royal emblem; and that then, at the beginning of the world, men had no other statues of the gods than spears, and therefore bowed down before these and worshipped them reverently. But after they began to make the gods in human form, they worshipped no longer the spears but the statues; nevertheless, in order still to preserve the memory of the ancient religion, they afterwards added spears to the sacred idols.

When Anchises in Virgil shows Aeneas his progeny that is to come, he begins with a youth leaning on a spear, and here Servius notes that the spear among the ancients was an honoured prize for those young men who, defeating the enemy in battle, had begun to show their valour. And likewise he says that the ancients esteemed the spear above all other arms, and that it was a sign of pre-eminence and of command, and was therefore given to valiant men; that things sold in public were sold under the spear; and that the Carthaginians, wanting war with the Romans, sent them a spear.
Suda

Suda reports that it was a custom in Athens that when someone who had been killed was carried to burial, the relatives who accompanied him had a spear carried with him, or planted it at the head of the grave, thereby making it known to the one who had killed him that he would not get past it without vengeance. So the spear was highly esteemed by the ancients, and among them was a very notable emblem. Hence it is no wonder that they often gave it to sacred statues.
Boccaccio

Of the chariot of Juno described by Homer it could be said that it signifies the various colours that are sometimes seen in the air; but Boccaccio holds otherwise, and says that it is made so richly because she was believed to be the goddess of riches, and that the arms given to her signify that for the most part men fight one another over riches.
Goddess of riches

And therefore they painted her with a sceptre in her hand, as though it were in her power to give riches and kingdoms, as she promised to do to Paris when she wanted to be judged by him the most beautiful of those two other goddesses. And this, as they say of the others too, is only too true, if by her we understand the earth, as Fulgentius writes, who depicts Juno with her head wrapped in a cloth and with a sceptre in her hand, showing by this that to rule is nothing other than to possess countries, and by the other that riches lie covered and hidden in the earth, because it holds in itself the veins of all the metals and in it the precious gems are found.
Peacock given to Juno

The peacock was given to this goddess as her own bird and consecrated to her. Hence Pausanias, describing the things that were in the temple of Juno in a certain part of Greece, says that there was a peacock there made entirely of gold and gleaming gems, offered and dedicated to the goddess by the emperor Hadrian as the bird consecrated to her; of which, besides the fable that is told of Argus, they say the cause is that riches draw our minds to themselves just as the peacock by its beauty draws to itself the eyes of onlookers.

And Boccaccio, where he recounts the progeny of the gods, makes a long discourse, wishing to show that the rich and powerful resemble the peacock in almost all their affairs, in that they speak proudly, are arrogant and always want to stand above others, like being praised, though falsely, and other similar things, which, as in Boccaccio's time, so today might well be found in many.
Birds given to Juno
Sign of nobility

Nor was the peacock alone given to Juno, but the ancients consecrated other birds to her as well, among which was a certain kind of hawk, and the vulture too, as Aelian says, according to the Egyptians, who for that reason crowned the statue of Isis with the feathers of this bird, because Isis was the same for them; and they also placed them around the entrances of houses; and Alexander ab Alexandro reports that in Egypt they did this as a sign of nobility and of the antiquity of the family.

The goose likewise was consecrated to Juno, and the Romans kept several in her temple, which were the best guard of the Capitol when the Gauls besieged it and would have got in there one night in secret, if these had not cried out; so they were afterwards fed there at public expense, and the censors in particular had charge of them, and one was made of silver in the same temple of Juno. And in order to show themselves duly grateful to this beast, which had done them so great a service, the Romans ordained that every year at a certain time a goose should be carried about the city with great ceremony on a handsome, well-adorned litter, and that at the same time a dog should be impaled, the stake being of elder, to punish it for the bad guard it kept on the Capitol, defended by the goose, as I have said.
Iris

Besides this, the poets said that Iris, who signifies the celestial rainbow, was the herald and messenger of Juno, and that she was the daughter of Thaumas, which signifies wonder, because when she appears she seems marvellous on account of the colours she shows, just as riches make fools marvel, and these go away as quickly as we see Iris vanish. She too was likewise called a goddess by the ancients, and was depicted in the form of a woman in a garment of various colours, and sometimes yellow, girt up all around, in order to be swifter on her way whenever her goddess commanded her, and with wings likewise of various colours, as Virgil said, where Juno sends her to cut Dido's fatal lock.
Image of Iris, messenger of Juno, daughter of Thaumas, or of wonder: by her colours a symbol of riches, which are a marvel to fools and quickly vanish.
Nymphs of Juno

Juno also had fourteen nymphs in her service, as in Virgil she says to Aeolus, promising him Deiopea, the most beautiful, as his wife, if he would let loose the winds, of which he was believed king, and send them to trouble the sea, so that Aeneas could not reach Italy. These, it is said, showed the changes of the air, which is understood by Juno, and the various incidents that appear in it, such as clear weather, gusts of wind, rains, snows, lightning flashes, thunders, mists and other such things.
Martianus Capella
Image of Jupiter [?]
qm: The marginal note beside Martianus's description of Juno reads "Imagine di Gioue" ("Image of Jupiter"), although the text describes Juno (Jupiter appears only in the comparison of the faces); translated as printed.

blocks.text: Martianus Capella likewise shows these same things when he imagines that Juno sits beneath Jupiter, and describes her in this way. She has her head covered with a certain bright and white veil, over which is a crown adorned with precious gems, such as the green Scythis, the fiery Ceraunius and the whitening Hyacinth, placed on it by Iris; her face almost always shines, and is very like her brother's, except that he is always cheerful and is never troubled, whereas Juno changes in countenance and sometimes shows a cloudy face. The garment that she has underneath seems of glass, clear and bright, but the cloak above is dark and murky, yet in such a way that if some light touches it, it shines; and a band of various colours girds her knees, which sometimes shines with wondrous beauty, and sometimes the variety of colours grows so thin that it no longer appears.
Hesiod

Her shoes are likewise of a dark colour, and have soles so black that they represent the darkness of night; although Hesiod imagines them to be gilded, and the other poets do the same. This goddess holds the thunderbolt in her right hand and a resounding tympanum in her left.
Statue of Juno

And this image shows the properties of the air, and what comes from it, so openly that there is no need to say more about it, and so I go on to give a great statue of Juno, which, as Pausanias writes, was in the country of Corinth, made of gold and ivory by Polykleitos, with a crown on its head on which the Horae and the Graces were carved with wonderful art; and in one hand she held a pomegranate and in the other a sceptre, on which a cuckoo sat; because, say the fables, Jupiter, once in love with Juno, changed himself into this bird, and she, in play, as young girls do, took it; and so he then had the opportunity to lie with her.

Image of Juno, queen of the gods, wife of Jupiter, understood as the air, and image of Juno of Corinth and of the bird the cuckoo, into which Jupiter changed himself when he first lay with the said goddess Juno, his sister.
Apuleius

To this Pausanias added that although he does not believe such things, nor the other similar ones that are told of the gods, he does not think they are to be scorned, as though he meant to say that they are mysterious and show something other than what the words sound like; but what meaning they have he does not say, and so I too do not say it, because I have already said several times that I do not wish to set down anything about which the ancients have not written. And although it may be that perhaps someone has already written of this, I have nevertheless not yet found it. But then Apuleius, when he describes the judgement of Paris performed on the stage, says that there came forth a young girl who resembled Juno, with a modest face, her head bound with a white diadem and a sceptre in her hand, accompanied by Castor and Pollux, who had on their heads a helmet with a crest of a star; and made thus they are seen on some ancient medals.
Castor and Pollux

We read that they were sons of Jupiter and so loving toward each other that, as the fables feigned, dividing life between them, they lived and died by turns, for which they deserved to be placed in Heaven, where they make the sign of the Gemini, which even today are figured by those who draw the things of Heaven in the way that the Lacedaemonians once made an idol of them; and it was in this fashion: they set two beams at an equal distance from each other, crossed likewise by two other beams, as if this image suited the equal love of the two brothers, of whom one was the strongest at wrestling and the other on horseback; so they were also sometimes depicted on two white horses, and these were perhaps the ones which they say Juno gave them, having herself had them first from Neptune, named one Xanthus, the other Cyllarus. And thus, on horseback, they were among the Athenians in a certain very ancient temple of theirs.
Justin
Locrians
Crotonians

In this way they also appeared to Vatinius, as Tullius writes, when he was returning from Rieti to Rome, and told him that on that day King Perseus had been taken prisoner. We also read, and Justin writes it, that in a certain battle in which fifteen thousand Locrians were victorious against a hundred and twenty thousand Crotonians, two young men appeared on two white horses, tall and handsome, armed differently from all the others, with purple garments about them, who fought valiantly before all the others on behalf of the Locrians, and vanished immediately after the victory. These were believed to be Castor and Pollux, because the Locrians, not having been able to get help from the Lacedaemonians, had asked help of them.
Pausanias

And how Castor and Pollux were represented was also shown by two Messenian youths, according to Pausanias, when with a cunning pretence they wished to deceive the Lacedaemonians on a day when they were solemnly celebrating their festival in the camp. For, having put on two white tunics with purple cloaks over them, and with spears in hand, on two most beautiful horses, they showed themselves suddenly. The Lacedaemonians thought that they were Castor and Pollux, come to the festival celebrated for them, and went out to meet them, all unarmed, worshipping them and praying that they would be willing to stay among them with a favourable numen, when the two youths, throwing themselves among them, wounding now these, now those, with their spears, killed many, and having made no small slaughter of the enemy, returned without being in the least hurt by them.

Besides this, Castor and Pollux had caps on their heads, as Festus Pompeius says, because they were from Laconia, where they used to go into battle with caps on their heads. And therefore Catullus in a certain epigram of his calls them Pileate brothers, because pileus, which is a Latin word, means cap in the vernacular. Pausanias likewise writes that in a certain place in Laconia there were some little figures wearing pilei, which he does not know very well whether they were made for the Castors (for under the name of the one the ancients understood both brothers), but he does think so.

Image of Castor and Pollux, gods of sailors, signifying calm at their appearance, who are also protectors of horses, being stars most swift in their course, and one of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, called the two twins, sons of Jupiter and Leda.
Sign of liberty

Nor shall I now fail to say that the pileus among the Romans was the badge of liberty, because it was their custom that when they wanted to give freedom to a slave they had his head shaved and gave him a cap to wear. This ceremony was performed in the temple of Feronia, because she was the goddess of those to whom freedom (*libertà*) was given, and they were called Libertini.
Plautus
Hence in Plautus a slave desirous of freedom speaks thus:

lines: May God grant that I may today, with shaven head, take the cap.
blocks.author: Plautus

blocks.text: And we read that in Rome, after Julius Caesar was killed, spears with the pileus on top were planted in the squares, wishing in that way to call the people and the whole city to their former liberty. When the Romans had need of soldiers, or when someone then wanted to stir up tumult and sedition, they called the slaves to the pileus, meaning thereby that they gave freedom to all, so that they would fight for it. Hence too it is that on certain ancient medals of Brutus a cap is seen placed above two daggers, showing thereby that he killed the tyrant and restored liberty to his country.

When Nero died, the populace in Rome, as Suetonius writes, and in the provinces as well, went about rejoicing with caps on their heads, wishing in that way to show that they were freed from grievous and cruel servitude. And we read in Plutarch that Lucius Terentius, a most noble Roman, went behind the triumph of Scipio with a cap on his head, as if he had been his freedman; and this because he had been freed by him from the Carthaginians, who had earlier taken him prisoner; and many Romans did the same in the triumph of Titus Quinctius, ransomed by him after he had conquered Macedonia, as, besides Plutarch, Livy also writes.

Besides this, the cap was a sign of virtue and of great learning, and for this reason it is still given today together with the title of doctor and master. And the ancients also sometimes put slaves up for sale with a cap on their heads, as Gellius reports, but only those who had no defect; so that the cap meant that the buyer could not be deceived, and that the seller was therefore free and was not afterwards bound to anything, as though it were a sure sign of the soundness and goodness of the slave sold.

But to return to the Castors: since, as I said, Pollux too is understood under this name, Bibulus, who was consul together with Caesar, made a jest of it when he saw that his colleague had so usurped all the authority of the consulship, and that whatever the two of them did was said to be done by Caesar alone, saying that what had happened to him was what happened to Pollux, who in the temple dedicated to him and to his brother had no name, because it was called the temple of Castor alone, or of the Castors.
Aelian
Why the Castors are called upon by sailors

These, then, were represented, as Aelian says and Suda reports, as tall young men, beardless, like one another, with military garments about them, with swords at their sides and spears in their hands, and in place of the stars I spoke of, they sometimes also put little flames on their heads. For we read that when the Argonauts were once strangely troubled by a heavy storm at sea, so that all feared to perish, and Orpheus had made vows for the safety of all, two stars, or flames, appeared above the head of the Castors, which gave them a sign of safety; and hence it came about afterwards that the Castors were called upon by sailors in their dangers.

Hence Pausanias, writing of a certain statue of Neptune which was among the Corinthians, says that on its base the Castors were carved, as those who were believed to be numina that bring safety to ships and to sailors. They were also believed to be certain stars, or lights, which, as Seneca and Pliny write, are accustomed to appear at sea in great storms and give a sign of calm. And since these show themselves in the air, and the air is represented by Juno, it was reasonable that the two brothers Castor and Pollux were placed in the company of this goddess.
Theopompus. Hellanicus

And of her the fables feign, as Theopompus and Hellanicus relate, that Jupiter once bound her feet with chains of gold, adding very heavy weights of iron, so that she hung in the air; wishing by this to signify that the lower part of the air, which is farthest from the element of fire and is therefore denser, where the clouds, the mists and other such things are formed, easily unites with water and earth, which are heavy elements and always descend.
Varro
The flammeum, veil of brides

We read in Pausanias that in a certain part of Boeotia there was a temple consecrated to Juno, in which was a very large idol of her, standing upright, and there she was called the bride. But it seems to me that she had this name with better reason on the island of Samos. For Varro writes, and Lactantius repeats it, that this island was first called Parthenia after Juno, who stayed there while she was a girl and a maiden, and was married there as well to Jupiter; and so in her temple there was a beautiful idol made in the form of a bride, which must have had that coloured veil with which new brides covered their faces, and it was called the flammeum, perhaps from the colour of flame, because it was red and showed that the girl who was to be joined to a man blushed with shame. So some have said of this veil, although some others hold that it should be understood otherwise, as I shall say later when I draw Hymenaeus.

And so Varro writes that the ancients observed the custom that newly married couples should come together only at night, as though honest girls would have less to be ashamed of in the darkness of night. And the brides went to the husband at night, carried in a litter by mules or oxen, as Suda writes; and the litter was made in such a way that the bride sat in the middle, the bridegroom on one side, and on the other the most honoured and dearest friend or relative he had, from which perhaps there has come today among us the custom for the bridegroom to find one of his dearest friends who, attending the wedding with him, is afterwards called “best man”.
Plutarch
Torches before brides

And before them, as can be gathered from Plutarch in his Questions, five boys carried as many lit torches, of pitch pine or of hawthorn; which torches, besides the service they performed in driving away the darkness of night, also gave by their light a sign and good omen of the offspring that was expected of that marriage, since to beget is nothing other than to bring forth into light.
Even and odd number

Nor could there be more than five, because according to some it was believed that a woman could bear up to five children at one birth, and no more. But others, considering the matter more subtly, have said that the ancients used the odd number at weddings as a sign of peace and union, because it cannot be divided into two equal parts without there always remaining one in the middle, which can afterwards join them together again, as common to both; so it was believed that the odd number is pleasing to the gods of Heaven, authors of peace and quiet, and the even to those of the Underworld, from whom come discord and disunion, just as the even number can be disunited by making two equal parts of it, with nothing remaining in the middle to reunite them.

And they took five, because this is the first number that arises from the union of the first two numbers, even and odd, which are three and two; for one is not a number, but a principle from which counting begins. And they likewise called upon five gods, and worshipped them with devout prayers. These were Jupiter and Juno adult, that is, no longer children; Venus, Suada and Diana.
Fire and water presented to the bride

Besides this, the ancients set before the new bride fire and water, either to show her that just as fire by itself can produce nothing, nor nourish it, having no moisture at all, and water still less, being wholly cold (for which reason, for the generation of animals and of all the other things produced by nature, heat and moisture must be joined together), so, to preserve the human race, it is necessary that man and woman be joined together; or to give her to understand, by the fire, which purges and separates the pure from the impure, and by the water, which washes out stains and takes away filth, that she must keep herself chaste, pure and clean, and guard herself against everything that can stain the laws of marriage.

They also made her carry the spindle and the distaff, and pass over a sheep's skin with all its wool the first time she entered her husband's house, and they used many other ceremonies; but let these few suffice for now, to give an idea of how Juno is to be depicted in the form of a bride, since Varro did not say it when he said that there was such an idol of hers on the island of Samos.
Juno as bride

But to return to what we said on the report of Pausanias, that Juno in Boeotia was called the bride, let us see the reason, as he gives it, who writes of it. Juno, angry with Jupiter, once left him and went to Euboea, that is Negroponte; and he, who nevertheless wished to placate her and make her return, but did not know in what way, asked advice of Cithaeron, then lord of that place, who suggested to him that he should have a statue made of oak and carry it about covered so that it could not be seen, pretending it to be a young girl whom he had newly made his bride.

So Jupiter did, and the new bride was already being led about, when Juno, who had learned of this and was greatly vexed by it, came out and drew near to the cart where she believed the new bride was hidden, and, full of jealousy and anger, tore the cloths that covered her, and finding it a wooden statue, rejoiced greatly and made peace with Jupiter, and stayed with him as a new bride. Hence the ancients afterwards celebrated some days of festival in memory of this fable, which Plutarch, as Eusebius reports, interprets in this way.

The discord that arose between Juno and Jupiter is nothing other than the unbalancing of the elements, from which comes the destruction of things; just as through their balance, or a certain proportion among them, the same things are born and preserved.
Oak, very useful

If Juno, then, that is moist and windy nature, is opposed to Jupiter [?], that is the hot and dry power, and scorns him, there will be as many rains, flooding the earth, as there once were in the country of Boeotia, which went wholly under the waters; and so, when these afterwards went down and the earth was left uncovered, the fables feigned that Jupiter and Juno were reconciled, and that the veils were torn and the statue of oak was seen. For they say that the first tree that sprang up out of the earth was the oak, which, as Hesiod says, was of double benefit to mortals, since from its branches they gathered the acorns on which they lived before, and from the trunk they made roofs.
qm: "Se Giunone adunque cioè la natura humida, & ventosa a Gioue, che è la virtù calda, & secca, & lo sprezza" — the verb governing "a Gioue" is missing in the source; rendered "is opposed to Jupiter", according to the sense.

blocks.text: Roses of Juno
Milky Way. Tertullian

For Juno the ancients made wreaths of white lilies, which they called the roses of Juno, because, tinted with her milk, they became white, as the fables relate, saying that Jupiter, while she slept, put Hercules, still a little child, to her breasts, so that, having nourished him with her milk, she should not hate him afterwards. But he, sucking too greedily, made the goddess wake; and recognising him, she at once thrust him away from her, so that the milk, which was still flowing, was for the most part scattered over Heaven and made there that certain white band which is still seen there, which the astrologers call the Milky Way, and the rest fell down to earth upon the lilies, which were left so tinted with white that ever since they have always been born white.

Tertullian writes that in Argos, a city of Greece, there was an idol of Juno encircled with vine branches, and which had under its feet the skin of a lion: as though she wished to have those branches in contempt of Bacchus, and this skin likewise in dishonour of Hercules, because she hated both of them greatly, being stepmother to both, according to the fables.

Image of Juno of Argos, of Juno the Saviour in Lanuvium, and of Juno, queen of the gods, patroness of the air, stepmother and hater of Bacchus and Hercules, purifier and cleanser of things, which is the proper effect of the air.
Titus Livy. Marcus Tullius

In Lanuvium, a city of Latium, Juno Sospita was worshipped, whom we can call the saviour, as the principal numen of that place, according to what Titus Livy relates; and she had her statue there, as Marcus Tullius writes, with the skin of a goat about her body, with a spear in one hand and a small shield in the other.
Juno of February. Festus

And Festus, speaking of Juno of February, of why she had this name, says that the Romans sacrificed to her in the month of February, and that the Lupercalia celebrated in this month were consecrated to her, in which the Luperci ran through the city and purified the women, who for this purpose held out their hand to them, and they struck them with that of which Juno's jerkin is made, which is the skins of goats.
Virgil
Vicus Iugarius. Juno Iugalis. Couples bound together

Besides this, it is found that the ancients sometimes made the statue of Juno also with shears in her hand, as Suda reports, and he gives the reason for it, saying that the air, understood by Juno, purges and cleanses, as shears, cutting the hair, make bodies smooth and clean. And on an ancient medal of the emperor Nerva is seen a matron crowned with rays, who sits on a high throne and holds a sceptre in her left hand and shears in her right. Many judged this to be Juno; nevertheless the letters that are on that medal call her the Fortune of the Roman people. Nor do I remember having seen or read of any other image or statue of Juno, except one made by some who know that the ancients called her the inventor of marriage, and that she had charge of weddings; hence Dido in Virgil, when she has decided to take Aeneas as her husband, sacrifices to certain gods, but before all to Juno:

lines: She who has charge of the marriage knot.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: These have depicted her standing, clothed, with poppy heads in her hand and a yoke at her feet, wishing to show by this how husband and wife must stay joined together, and by the heads the numerous offspring that then follows. Of this I find no mention in any of the ancients, but I do find that in Rome a certain place was called Vicus Iugarius, because Juno is called Iugalis, as if by the favour of her numen man and woman were joined (*si giungessero*) together; she had an altar there, to which the newly married went, and were bound together by the priest with certain knots, giving them thereby to understand that their minds should always be bound thus in one will, as their bodies were then by those knots.
Marriage
Hymenaeus

Hence it came about that some, perhaps taking the example from this, and from what can be seen in the image of Venus made in fetters, have depicted marriage with a yoke on the neck and with fetters on the feet. Some have held that this was introduced first by Juno, as I have said, some by Venus, and some others by Hymenaeus, who was therefore worshipped as the god of weddings, at which they invoked him with certain solemn prayers, that he might be favourable to them and give them a happy outcome by his numen.

Image of Juno, inventor or protector of marriage, called Juno Iugalis, and of the yoke and the birds sacred to her, signifying the duty of the married and the succession, or offspring, that comes from a harmonious marriage.
Gall thrown away

But we read also that the ancients, showing by many ceremonies the peace and union that ought to be between husband and wife, and desiring for them every good and consolation, in celebrating weddings named nothing except what could give good omen and a sign of happiness. Hence they also often called upon the crow, as is seen in the image of Concord; and sacrificing to Juno Iugalis they cut the gall out of the victim and threw it behind the altar, to show that between husband and wife there must be no bitterness of hatred, nor any anger.
Tale of Hymenaeus

And for this reason some hold that Hymenaeus too was invoked, not because he had ordained marriage, but because after many labours and grave dangers he obtained the wedding he desired, with a most happy outcome; and the tale is this. Hymenaeus was a youth in Athens, son of Apollo and of Calliope, one of the nine Muses, so beautiful, and with a face so delicate, that by many he was thought to be a woman, and he fell most ardently in love with a beautiful and most noble girl, and without hoping ever to enjoy her love, because he was, by family, far too inferior in blood and riches to the girl, he went about nourishing himself as best he could on the sight of the beloved, and followed her always and wherever he was allowed and permitted to go, and he often found himself among the other girls so arrayed (his smooth cheek helping him much in this) that he was easily taken for one of them.

While the poor boy was thus deceiving others, but even more himself, it happened that he was carried off with his beloved, and with many other most noble girls of Athens, who had gone together outside the city for the sacrifices of Eleusinian Ceres, by pirates who arrived there suddenly. These, when they were many miles away from Athens, pleased with their booty, put in to land, and withdrawing to a certain place where they felt safe, tired already from the continual sailing, fell asleep. Then Hymenaeus, seizing the occasion to free himself and the abducted girls, killed them all before any of them woke, and having put the girls back in a safe place, returned to the city and promised the Athenians to restore to them their already lost daughters, if they would give him as wife the one he loved so much.

This was readily granted him, since it seemed to everyone that he had well deserved her. And so Hymenaeus had the girl he had so much desired. Having celebrated a solemn and joyful wedding, he lived afterwards with her happily all his life. Since, then, these maidens were recovered by him, and the marriage that had been so desired had a happy outcome, the ancients often repeated his name at weddings for good omen, as if they wished for those who were marrying the happiness of Hymenaeus.
Thalassius, called upon at weddings

And this was a custom of the Greeks, just as it was of the Romans to call upon Thalassius at weddings, likewise for good omen. For, as Livy writes, when the Sabine women were carried off by the Romans, a most beautiful girl fell into the hands of a poor soldier, and when asked, he said that he was taking her to Thalassius, because he had already seen that someone had cast an eye on her in order to take her from him.
